title: Optimization
body:
Finding the largest or smallest value a quantity can take. This is the application the rest of the
degree cares about: **train a model** means minimise a [[Loss Function]], and that is this note
with more variables.

The idea is one line. At an interior maximum or minimum the tangent line is flat, so
$f'(x) = 0$. Solve that, check the candidates, done.

## Local versus absolute

A **local** extremum beats its immediate neighbours. An **absolute** (global) extremum beats every
point in the domain. They are different questions and the second is the one word problems ask.

> **Extreme Value Theorem**: a [[Continuity|continuous]] function on a **closed, bounded** interval
> $[a,b]$ attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.

Both hypotheses are load-bearing. On the open interval $(0,1)$, $f(x) = x$ attains neither. On
$[0,\infty)$, $f(x) = x$ attains no maximum. Discontinuous functions can miss out too. When the
theorem applies, the search is finite:

## The closed-interval method

1. Find the critical points in $(a,b)$: where $f' = 0$ or $f'$ does not exist
2. Evaluate $f$ at every critical point **and at both endpoints**
3. Biggest value wins, smallest value wins

No derivative test is needed, because comparing the actual values settles it. Forgetting the
endpoints is the classic error, and it is the one the theorem is warning you about.

On an **open** interval or an unbounded domain there are no endpoints to check, so you do need the
first or [[Curve Sketching|second derivative test]], plus the limits at the ends of the domain, to
argue that a local extremum is global.

## Word problems

The calculus is the easy half. The modelling is the work:

1. Draw it, name the variables
2. Write the quantity to be optimised as a formula (the **objective**)
3. Use the constraint to eliminate variables until the objective is a function of **one** variable
4. State the domain that physically makes sense, which is where the interval comes from
5. Optimise

"Largest area with 100 m of fence" is objective $A = xy$, constraint $2x + 2y = 100$, substitute to
$A(x) = x(50 - x)$ on $[0,50]$, and $A'(x) = 50 - 2x = 0$ gives $x = 25$. A square. The answer to
every unconstrained-shape fencing problem is a square, and the point of doing it is the elimination
step, not the answer.

## Where this goes

[[Gradient Descent]] is this problem when step 3 is impossible. With one variable you set $f' = 0$
and solve. With a million weights in a [[Neural Network]] there is no closed form, so instead you
evaluate the [[Gradient]] (the vector of [[Partial Derivative|partial derivatives]], the
multivariable $f'$) and step downhill by a small amount, repeatedly. Same criterion, since a
minimum still has zero gradient; different algorithm, because you can only reach it iteratively.

[[Least Squares]] and [[Linear Regression]] are the happy case in between: many variables, but the
objective is quadratic, so setting the derivative to zero gives a linear system with an answer you
can write down. [[Gradient Descent]] exists for everything else.

## Related

- [[Multivariable Optimization]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]: this note with several inputs, where
  $f' = 0$ becomes $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ and a new outcome appears, the saddle point.
  [[Lagrange Multipliers]] is what step 3 above becomes when the constraint cannot be eliminated
- [[Curve Sketching]]: same derivative tests, read as a shape rather than a single value
- [[Mean Value Theorem]]: what makes "$f' = 0$ throughout means constant" a theorem
